Remote libSQL and Turso

Source: vignettes/libsql.Rmd
libsql.Rmd

libSQL is based on SQLite and can run as a remote database server. Turso offers hosted endpoints with compatible SQL APIs. Use oauth_db_libsql_api() to run SQLite SQL against a remote libSQL or compatible Turso endpoint. shinyOAuth manages the visitor’s sign-in and token renewal; the database endpoint checks their token and permissions. This helper uses the Hrana HTTP API, without an additional R database driver.

A local SQLite file has no OAuth login. The endpoint must be a server configured to accept the access tokens issued to your app.

Try self-hosted libSQL locally

Start Docker and run:

shinyOAuthDB::oauth_db_demo("libsql")

The package includes libSQL 0.24.33, a Shiny app and a Keycloak configuration that issues compatible Ed25519-signed access tokens. Alice and Bob both receive id=default and a=ro, with no access-token audience. They can read the shared sample table; Try a write confirms that libSQL refuses writes. See Local Docker demos for passwords and cleanup.

Use oauth_db_demo("libsql", action = "files") to inspect realm-extended.json and libsql/server.py. A separate provisioning client seeds the table; the Shiny client requests read-only tokens. This example runs self-hosted libSQL; Turso Cloud uses the different setup below.

Before running the app

The endpoint must accept visitor access tokens from your provider. Turso Cloud’s external-provider setup and self-hosted libSQL use different token formats; the compatibility section after the app explains both.

Setting Where to get it
OAUTHDB_LIBSQL_URL Turso database details or turso db show your-database --url; for self-hosting, your server’s HTTPS URL
OAUTHDB_LIBSQL_ISSUER The provider configured to issue compatible database tokens
Client ID and secret Your OAuth app registration
OAUTHDB_LIBSQL_AUDIENCE The provider’s API audience, if required; leave empty for the self-hosted format below
sqlite.read An example scope your provider must define or replace

Save these values in .Renviron and restart R. The client uses the HTTP API and needs no extra R database driver. A local SQLite file has no OAuth login.

A complete app

Replace the table name and scopes for your database. The provider’s token configuration must satisfy the requirements above before running the app.

library(shiny)
library(shinyOAuth)
library(shinyOAuthDB)

audience <- Sys.getenv("OAUTHDB_LIBSQL_AUDIENCE")
provider <- oauth_provider_oidc_discover(
  issuer = Sys.getenv("OAUTHDB_LIBSQL_ISSUER"),
  extra_auth_params = if (nzchar(audience)) {
    list(audience = audience)
  } else {
    list()
  }
)
client <- oauth_client(
  provider,
  client_id = Sys.getenv("OAUTHDB_CLIENT_ID"),
  client_secret = Sys.getenv("OAUTHDB_CLIENT_SECRET"),
  redirect_uri = "http://localhost:8100",
  scopes = c("openid", "sqlite.read")
)

ui <- oauth_ui(
  fluidPage(
    actionButton("login", "Sign in"),
    actionButton("logout", "Sign out"),
    tableOutput("rows")
  ),
  id = "auth",
  client = client
)

server <- function(input, output, session) {
  auth <- oauth_module_server("auth", client, auto_redirect = FALSE)
  observeEvent(input$login, auth$request_login())
  observeEvent(input$logout, auth$logout())

  libsql <- oauth_db_libsql_api(
    auth$connection,
    url = Sys.getenv("OAUTHDB_LIBSQL_URL"),
    required_scopes = "sqlite.read"
  )
  output$rows <- renderTable({
    libsql$query(
      "SELECT id, total FROM orders WHERE country = :country LIMIT 20",
      parameters = list(country = "NL")
    )
  })
}

runApp(
  shinyApp(ui, server, uiPattern = ".*"),
  port = 8100,
  launch.browser = FALSE
)

# Open the app in your regular browser at http://localhost:8100
# (viewers in RStudio/Positron/etc. cannot perform necessary redirects)

Run source("example.R"). The app waits for sign-in before sending SQL and clears the output on sign-out. Request offline_access too if your provider requires it to renew tokens.

Configure a compatible token issuer

Self-hosted libSQL

The tested open-source libSQL server, version 0.24.33, verifies Ed25519 signatures using SQLD_AUTH_JWT_KEY_FILE or SQLD_AUTH_JWT_KEY. Configure the public verification key using the server’s Docker authentication instructions. The app must obtain compatible database access tokens from its issuer.

Issue an explicit database namespace in id, permissions in a ("ro" for read-only or "rw" for read/write), and an exp expiry. Do not rely on omitted claims: the tested server defaults missing permissions to write access and permits tokens without an expiry. Its newer p permission format is another option; see the server token implementation.

This configuration is not a general OIDC resource server. It has no issuer/audience discovery settings or JWKS URL configuration like the DuckDB quack_oauth server. The tested version rejects tokens with an aud claim because no accepted audience is configured. Use a dedicated signing key and restrict token issuance to this database and the intended users. The issuer must support Ed25519 signing and the required database claims. Existing Entra, Google or default Auth0 tokens cannot simply be reused.

If your identity provider cannot issue compatible database access tokens, you need a separate authorization gateway or token-exchange service. This helper does not mint database tokens or implement token exchange.

Put the server behind HTTPS. Pass ca_bundle for a private CA. On Windows, the Docker acceptance test uses curl’s OpenSSL backend for its temporary CA bundle. If your curl/Schannel build rejects a supplied private CA, set CURL_SSL_BACKEND=openssl before loading curl or shinyOAuthDB and restart R. Keep certificate and hostname verification enabled.

Turso Cloud external providers

Turso Cloud has a separate external authentication setup. Its current documentation lists Clerk and Auth0 as supported providers. Register the provider’s JWKS endpoint and use the Turso CLI to generate a database-specific JWT claims template, then configure the provider to issue those claims. Restrict the template to the required database and operations.

The resulting provider-issued access token goes directly to the database endpoint. A Turso platform-management API token, a shared database token, or an OIDC ID token does not represent the visitor’s database authorization. Confirm the selected provider flow supplies the compatible database access token through shinyOAuth’s auth$connection.

Configure the app

Register an OAuth client with redirect URI http://localhost:8100. Request the database’s configured permissions and any provider-specific audience parameter. sqlite.read below is an example OAuth scope that your issuer must define; libSQL’s a or p claims enforce database permissions. Remove or replace that scope if your registration uses another scheme.

Save the following values in .Renviron and restart R:

OAUTHDB_CLIENT_ID=your-client-id
OAUTHDB_CLIENT_SECRET=your-client-secret
OAUTHDB_LIBSQL_ISSUER=https://your-provider.example.org/
OAUTHDB_LIBSQL_URL=libsql://your-database-your-org.turso.io
OAUTHDB_LIBSQL_AUDIENCE=your-provider-api-audience

The audience setting is for provider configurations such as Auth0 with Turso Cloud. Leave it empty for a self-hosted issuer configured to issue database tokens without an audience claim.

Parameters and result types

Use an unnamed list for positional ? parameters, or a fully named list for named parameters. Values travel separately from SQL; no interpolation is needed.

libsql$query("SELECT * FROM orders WHERE country = ?", list("NL"))
libsql$execute(
  "INSERT INTO events(value) VALUES (:value)",
  list(value = "signed in")
)
libsql$query("SELECT ? AS exact_integer", list(I("9223372036854775807")))
libsql$query("SELECT ? AS bytes, ? AS missing", list(as.raw(c(0, 255)), NULL))

Ordinary character values bind as text. Logical values bind as integers 1 or 0, and NULL or scalar NA bind as SQL NULL. Numeric values must be finite. Format dates and timestamps as strings in your database’s format.

SQLite integers return as strings so all 64 bits survive. Floating-point values remain numeric. Blobs are raw vectors in list columns. A column containing different non-null SQLite types remains a list, including nulls. All-null and empty columns use logical missing values and retain their names.

query(..., raw = TRUE) returns the validated Hrana statement result, including column declarations, affected-row count and last inserted row ID. execute() returns this metadata invisibly, without collecting result rows.

Request lifetime

Each operation obtains a current token, opens a new stream, executes one statement and closes the stream in the same HTTPS request. Calls do not share transactions, temporary tables, pragmas or other connection state. BEGIN and COMMIT across separate calls cannot form a transaction. This helper does not expose a DBI connection, batch transactions, cursors or embedded replicas.

Results arriving after an account change, lost required permissions, sign-out or session end are discarded. SQL requests are never replayed, including HTTP 401, timeouts and lost write responses. After an ambiguous write failure, check the database before deciding whether to submit again. A submitted statement may finish even if the Shiny session has ended.

The source checkout includes a libSQL Docker fixture. Run Rscript --vanilla tools/check-libsql-oauth.R from the repository root with Docker running and the test dependencies installed to check signed tokens, permissions, TLS, bound values and lost write responses locally. The fixture uses synthetic Shiny authorizations and does not test browser sign-in or Turso Cloud.
